claim: Adulis was located on the Red Sea coast in present-day Eritrea.
source: Adulis, located on the Red Sea coast in present-day Eritrea, was a bustling trading centre between the first and seventh centuries CE.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract and introduction of the manuscript.

claim: Adulis was a bustling trading centre between the first and seventh centuries CE.
source: Adulis, located on the Red Sea coast in present-day Eritrea, was a bustling trading centre between the first and seventh centuries CE.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract, supported by historical references.

claim: Agatharchides of Cnidus, Pliny the Elder, and Strabo noted the value of Adulis to Greco-Roman Egypt.
source: Several classical geographers—Agatharchides of Cnidus, Pliny the Elder, Strabo—noted the value of Adulis to Greco-Roman Egypt, particularly as an emporium for living animals, including baboons (Papio spp.).
evidence: References to classical geographers and their writings about Adulis.

claim: Adulis was particularly valued as an emporium for living animals, including baboons (Papio spp.).
source: Several classical geographers—Agatharchides of Cnidus, Pliny the Elder, Strabo—noted the value of Adulis to Greco-Roman Egypt, particularly as an emporium for living animals, including baboons (Papio spp.).
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract, supported by classical sources.

claim: Mummified baboons from Gabbanat el-Qurud are dated to ca. 800–540 BCE.
source: Dated to ca. 800–540 BCE, these animals could extend the antiquity of Egyptian–Adulite trade by as much as five centuries.
evidence: Radiometric dating evidence cited in the manuscript.

claim: Baboons from Gabbanat el-Qurud could extend the antiquity of Egyptian–Adulite trade by as much as five centuries.
source: Dated to ca. 800–540 BCE, these animals could extend the antiquity of Egyptian–Adulite trade by as much as five centuries.
evidence: Inference based on the dating of the mummified baboons and historical context.

claim: Dominy et al. (2020) used stable isotope analysis to show that two New Kingdom specimens of Papio hamadryas originate from the Horn of Africa.
source: Previously, Dominy et al. (2020) used stable isotope analysis to show that two New Kingdom specimens of Papio hamadryas originate from the Horn of Africa.
evidence: Direct citation of prior research findings.

claim: The study reports the complete mitochondrial genomes from a mummified baboon from Gabbanat el-Qurud and 14 museum specimens with known provenance.
source: Here, we report the complete mitochondrial genomes from a mummified baboon from Gabbanat el-Qurud and 14 museum specimens with known provenance together with published georeferenced mitochondrial sequence data.
evidence: Description of the data generated in this study.

claim: Phylogenetic assignment connects the mummified baboon to modern populations of P. hamadryas in Eritrea, Ethiopia, and eastern Sudan.
source: Phylogenetic assignment connects the mummified baboon to modern populations of P. hamadryas in Eritrea, Ethiopia, and eastern Sudan.
evidence: Result from phylogenetic analysis presented in the study.

claim: The result corroborates Greco-Roman historiographies by pointing toward present-day Eritrea, and by extension Adulis, as a source of baboons for Late Period Egyptians.
source: This result, assuming geographical stability of phylogenetic clades, corroborates Greco-Roman historiographies by pointing toward present-day Eritrea, and by extension Adulis, as a source of baboons for Late Period Egyptians.
evidence: Interpretation of phylogenetic results in historical context.

claim: The finding establishes geographic continuity with baboons from the fabled Land of Punt (Dominy et al., 2020).
source: It also establishes geographic continuity with baboons from the fabled Land of Punt (Dominy et al., 2020), giving weight to speculation that Punt and Adulis were essentially the same trading centres separated by a thousand years of history.
evidence: Inference connecting current findings with previous research.

claim: The finding gives weight to speculation that Punt and Adulis were essentially the same trading centres separated by a thousand years of history.
source: It also establishes geographic continuity with baboons from the fabled Land of Punt (Dominy et al., 2020), giving weight to speculation that Punt and Adulis were essentially the same trading centres separated by a thousand years of history.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on data and historical context.

claim: Trade at Adulis peaked between the fourth and seventh centuries CE.
source: Trade peaked between the fourth and seventh centuries CE, propelling the rise and expansion of the Aksumite kingdom, but its occupation history extends, at minimum, to the first millennium BCE (Zazzaro et al., 2014).
evidence: Historical information supported by citation.

claim: The occupation history of Adulis extends, at minimum, to the first millennium BCE (Zazzaro et al., 2014).
source: Trade peaked between the fourth and seventh centuries CE, propelling the rise and expansion of the Aksumite kingdom, but its occupation history extends, at minimum, to the first millennium BCE (Zazzaro et al., 2014).
evidence: Archaeological evidence cited from Zazzaro et al., 2014.

claim: Cosmas Indicopleustes visited Adulis in 518 CE.
source: In Topographia Christiana, a sixth-century text, the Nestorian merchant Cosmas Indicopleustes recounts his own visit to Adulis in 518 CE (Fauvelle-Aymar, 2009; Hatke, 2013).
evidence: Historical account from primary source cited in the manuscript.

claim: Cosmas Indicopleustes copied the text of a stele inscribed in Greek known today as the Monumentum Adulitanum I.
source: There he copied the text of a stele inscribed in Greek and known today as the Monumentum Adulitanum I.
evidence: Historical account from cited sources.

claim: The Monumentum Adulitanum I celebrates the military conquests of Ptolemy III Euergetes (reign: 246–222 BCE).
source: The text celebrates the military conquests of Ptolemy III Euergetes (reign: 246–222 BCE) and notes the local availability of war elephants for himself and his predecessor, Ptolemy II Philadelphus (reign: 284–246 BCE) (Bowersock, 2013).
evidence: Historical information from cited source.

claim: The Monumentum Adulitanum I notes the local availability of war elephants for Ptolemy III Euergetes and his predecessor, Ptolemy II Philadelphus (reign: 284–246 BCE) (Bowersock, 2013).
source: The text celebrates the military conquests of Ptolemy III Euergetes (reign: 246–222 BCE) and notes the local availability of war elephants for himself and his predecessor, Ptolemy II Philadelphus (reign: 284–246 BCE) (Bowersock, 2013).
evidence: Historical information from cited source.

claim: The Periplus Maris Erythraei is a first-century anonymous text focused on maritime trade across the Red Sea Basin.
source: Echoing this account is the first-century Periplus Maris Erythraei, an anonymous text focused on maritime trade across the Red Sea Basin: 'practically the whole number of elephants and rhinoceros that are killed live in the places inland, although at rare intervals they are hunted on the seacoast even near Adulis' (Casson, 1989; Casson, 1993).
evidence: Description of historical text with citation.

claim: According to the Periplus Maris Erythraei, elephants and rhinoceros were hunted on the seacoast near Adulis at rare intervals (Casson, 1989; Casson, 1993).
source: Echoing this account is the first-century Periplus Maris Erythraei, an anonymous text focused on maritime trade across the Red Sea Basin: 'practically the whole number of elephants and rhinoceros that are killed live in the places inland, although at rare intervals they are hunted on the seacoast even near Adulis' (Casson, 1989; Casson, 1993).
evidence: Direct quote from historical source with citation.

claim: Pliny the Elder described Adulis as a thriving emporium in his Naturalis Historia.
source: Pliny the Elder described Adulis as a thriving emporium in his Naturalis Historia, another first-century text, and commented on the availability of ivory, rhinoceros horn, hippopotamus hides, tortoise shell, and sphingia—or 'sphinx monkeys,' a term that probably refers to the gelada, Theropithecus gelada (Jolly and Ucko, 1969).
evidence: Historical account from Pliny the Elder cited in the manuscript.

claim: Pliny the Elder commented on the availability of ivory, rhinoceros horn, hippopotamus hides, tortoise shell, and sphingia at Adulis.
source: Pliny the Elder described Adulis as a thriving emporium in his Naturalis Historia, another first-century text, and commented on the availability of ivory, rhinoceros horn, hippopotamus hides, tortoise shell, and sphingia—or 'sphinx monkeys,' a term that probably refers to the gelada, Theropithecus gelada (Jolly and Ucko, 1969).
evidence: Historical account from Pliny the Elder cited in the manuscript.

claim: The term 'sphingia' or 'sphinx monkeys' probably refers to the gelada, Theropithecus gelada (Jolly and Ucko, 1969).
source: Pliny the Elder described Adulis as a thriving emporium in his Naturalis Historia, another first-century text, and commented on the availability of ivory, rhinoceros horn, hippopotamus hides, tortoise shell, and sphingia—or 'sphinx monkeys,' a term that probably refers to the gelada, Theropithecus gelada (Jolly and Ucko, 1969).
evidence: Interpretation of historical term supported by citation.

claim: Pliny's account relied heavily on the writings of Agatharchides of Cnidus (ca. 145 BCE).
source: Pliny's account relied heavily on the writings of Agatharchides of Cnidus (ca. 145 BCE), who described 'Aithiopia' (meaning the Red Sea coast and African hinterlands) as a source of sphinx monkeys, cepi (probably patas monkeys, Erythrocebus patas; Burstein, 1989), and cynocephali—or 'dog-heads.'
evidence: Historical relationship between sources.

claim: Agatharchides of Cnidus described 'Aithiopia' (meaning the Red Sea coast and African hinterlands) as a source of sphinx monkeys, cepi (probably patas monkeys, Erythrocebus patas; Burstein, 1989), and cynocephali.
source: Pliny's account relied heavily on the writings of Agatharchides of Cnidus (ca. 145 BCE), who described 'Aithiopia' (meaning the Red Sea coast and African hinterlands) as a source of sphinx monkeys, cepi (probably patas monkeys, Erythrocebus patas; Burstein, 1989), and cynocephali—or 'dog-heads.'
evidence: Historical account with interpretation and citation.

claim: The term 'cepi' probably refers to patas monkeys, Erythrocebus patas (Burstein, 1989).
source: Pliny's account relied heavily on the writings of Agatharchides of Cnidus (ca. 145 BCE), who described 'Aithiopia' (meaning the Red Sea coast and African hinterlands) as a source of sphinx monkeys, cepi (probably patas monkeys, Erythrocebus patas; Burstein, 1989), and cynocephali—or 'dog-heads.'
evidence: Interpretation of historical term supported by citation.

claim: Strabo's Geographica references the worship of cynocephali at Hermopolis (Egypt).
source: Strabo's Geographica references the worship of cynocephali at Hermopolis (Egypt), making it clear that the animal in question is the hamadryas baboon (Papio hamadryas), the traditional sacred animal of the Egyptian god Thoth (Figure 1).
evidence: Historical reference from Strabo's work.

claim: The cynocephali referenced by Strabo is the hamadryas baboon (Papio hamadryas).
source: Strabo's Geographica references the worship of cynocephali at Hermopolis (Egypt), making it clear that the animal in question is the hamadryas baboon (Papio hamadryas), the traditional sacred animal of the Egyptian god Thoth (Figure 1).
evidence: Interpretation of historical reference.

claim: The hamadryas baboon (Papio hamadryas) is the traditional sacred animal of the Egyptian god Thoth.
source: Strabo's Geographica references the worship of cynocephali at Hermopolis (Egypt), making it clear that the animal in question is the hamadryas baboon (Papio hamadryas), the traditional sacred animal of the Egyptian god Thoth (Figure 1).
evidence: Historical and cultural knowledge, supported by Figure 1.

claim: The current distribution of baboons excludes Egypt.
source: The source of baboons in ancient Egypt is an enduring question (Dominy et al., 2020) as the current distribution of baboons excludes Egypt (Figure 2) and there is no prehistoric evidence of baboons occurring in Egypt naturally (Geraads, 1987).
evidence: Stated directly and shown in Figure 2.

claim: There is no prehistoric evidence of baboons occurring in Egypt naturally (Geraads, 1987).
source: The source of baboons in ancient Egypt is an enduring question (Dominy et al., 2020) as the current distribution of baboons excludes Egypt (Figure 2) and there is no prehistoric evidence of baboons occurring in Egypt naturally (Geraads, 1987).
evidence: Cited from Geraads, 1987.

claim: The sanctuary and temple complex featured several 35-tonne statues of P. hamadryas as the embodiment of Thoth.
source: The sanctuary and temple complex featured several 35-tonne statues of P. hamadryas as the embodiment of Thoth.
evidence: Caption of Figure 1 describing the statues.

claim: Thoth is best known as a god of writing and wisdom, a lunar deity, and vizier of the gods, but also as a cosmic deity, creator god, and warrior (Stadler, 2012).
source: One of the oldest deities in the Egyptian pantheon, Thoth is best known as a god of writing and wisdom, a lunar deity, and vizier of the gods, but also as a cosmic deity, creator god, and warrior (Stadler, 2012).
evidence: Description of Thoth with citation.

claim: The quartzite statues were erected by Amenhotep III, 18th Dynasty, New Kingdom, 1390–1353 BCE.
source: The quartzite statues were erected by Amenhotep III, 18th Dynasty, New Kingdom, 1390–1353 BCE.
evidence: Caption of Figure 1 providing historical context.

claim: Introgressive hybridization has led to discordances between species assignment and mitochondrial clades.
source: Note that introgressive hybridization has led to discordances between species assignment and mitochondrial clades.
evidence: Note in Figure 2 caption explaining genetic patterns.

claim: Gabbanat el-Qurud is located ca. 2.5 km north–northwest of Medinet Habu, the mortuary temple of Ramses III.
source: In Topography of Thebes, Wilkinson, 1853 noted a site called Gabbanat el-Qurud ('Valley of the Monkeys') located ca. 2.5 km north–northwest of Medinet Habu, the mortuary temple of Ramses III.
evidence: Historical description from Wilkinson, 1853.

claim: French Egyptologists Louis Lortet and Claude Gaillard found Gabbanat el-Qurud in February 1905.
source: Intrigued by this observation, French Egyptologists Louis Lortet and Claude Gaillard sought and found the site in February 1905, along with the remains of mummified baboons.
evidence: Historical account of the discovery.

claim: Lortet and Gaillard recovered '17 skulls and a large quantity of bones' from Gabbanat el-Qurud.
source: They recovered '17 skulls and a large quantity of bones,' which they attributed to Papio anubis and P. hamadryas (Lortet and Gaillard, 1907).
evidence: Historical account from Lortet and Gaillard, 1907.

claim: Lortet and Gaillard attributed the recovered remains to Papio anubis and P. hamadryas (Lortet and Gaillard, 1907).
source: They recovered '17 skulls and a large quantity of bones,' which they attributed to Papio anubis and P. hamadryas (Lortet and Gaillard, 1907).
evidence: Historical taxonomic identification from Lortet and Gaillard, 1907.

claim: The assemblage from Gabbanat el-Qurud includes juvenile and adult males and females buried in jars, sarcophagi, or wooden coffins.
source: The assemblage includes juvenile and adult males and females buried in jars, sarcophagi, or wooden coffins.
evidence: Description of the archaeological assemblage.

claim: The linen wrapping of one mummified individual (MHNL 90001206) was dated radiometrically to 803–544 cal. BC (95.4%) (Richardin et al., 2017).
source: Now accessioned in the Musée des Confluences, Lyon, France, the linen wrapping of one mummified individual (MHNL 90001206) was dated radiometrically to 803–544 cal. BC (95.4%) (Richardin et al., 2017).
evidence: Radiometric dating result from Richardin et al., 2017.

claim: Ottoni et al., 2019 sampled dental calculus from 16 individuals in the Gabbanat el-Qurud assemblage.
source: Ottoni et al., 2019 sampled dental calculus from 16 individuals in this same assemblage and reported the preservation of ancient microbial DNA in a subset of six.
evidence: Citation of prior research on the same assemblage.

claim: Ottoni et al., 2019 reported the preservation of ancient microbial DNA in a subset of six individuals from Gabbanat el-Qurud.
source: Ottoni et al., 2019 sampled dental calculus from 16 individuals in this same assemblage and reported the preservation of ancient microbial DNA in a subset of six.
evidence: Citation of prior research findings.

claim: The study extracted DNA from the remaining tooth material of ten individuals from Gabbanat el-Qurud.
source: Their success motivated us to extract DNA from the remaining tooth material of ten individuals (Table 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Description of the current study's methods.

claim: The study obtained samples (skin, bone, or tooth) from 21 modern historic specimens of baboons available in museum collections.
source: In addition, we obtained samples (skin, bone, or tooth) from 21 modern historic specimens of baboons available in museum collections and representing the northeast African distribution of Papio (Table 1, Figure 2).
evidence: Description of the current study's sampling.

claim: The historic specimens were collected between 1855 and 1978.
source: These specimens were collected between 1855 and 1978, and we denote them 'historic samples' in the remainder of the article to distinguish them both from the older mummified specimens ('mummified samples') and recently collected material ('modern samples').
evidence: Description of sample collection dates.

claim: The study succeeded in sequencing the mitogenomes of 14 historic baboons from northeastern Africa and a mummified baboon recovered from Gabbanat el-Qurud.
source: We succeeded in sequencing the mitogenomes of 14 historic baboons from northeastern Africa and a mummified baboon recovered from Gabbanat el-Qurud, presenting the first genetic data of a mummified baboon from ancient Egypt to date.
evidence: Summary of the study's main results.

claim: This study presents the first genetic data of a mummified baboon from ancient Egypt to date.
source: We succeeded in sequencing the mitogenomes of 14 historic baboons from northeastern Africa and a mummified baboon recovered from Gabbanat el-Qurud, presenting the first genetic data of a mummified baboon from ancient Egypt to date.
evidence: Statement of novelty of the research.

claim: DNA of the mummified baboon shows post-mortem damage.
source: DNA of the mummified baboon shows post-mortem damage, which is, however, relatively low compared to what can be expected for samples of similar age (Dabney et al., 2013b, Kistler et al., 2017).
evidence: Analysis of DNA damage patterns in the mummified sample.

claim: The post-mortem damage in the mummified baboon DNA is relatively low compared to what can be expected for samples of similar age (Dabney et al., 2013b, Kistler et al., 2017).
source: DNA of the mummified baboon shows post-mortem damage, which is, however, relatively low compared to what can be expected for samples of similar age (Dabney et al., 2013b, Kistler et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparison of observed damage with expected levels from literature.

claim: Low frequencies of post-mortem damage have been attributed to the water deprivation during the mummification process, which may prevent hydrolytic deamination (Rossi et al., 2021).
source: Low frequencies of post-mortem damage were observed for aDNA from mummified specimens and have been attributed to the water deprivation during the mummification process, which may prevent hydrolytic deamination (Rossi et al., 2021).
evidence: Explanation of low damage based on cited research.

claim: Post-mortem damage observed in this study is within the range previously reported for aDNA derived from mummified Egyptians (Schuenemann et al., 2017) and sheep recovered from an Iranian saltmine (Rossi et al., 2021).
source: Post-mortem damage observed here is within the range previously reported for aDNA derived from mummified Egyptians (Schuenemann et al., 2017) and sheep recovered from an Iranian saltmine (Rossi et al., 2021), which supports the authentic origin of our ancient sequence data and tends to rule out the possibility of contamination with modern DNA.
evidence: Comparison with published data to validate authenticity.

claim: The low frequency of mismatches in the mapped reads from the mummified sample and its unique sequence are evidence against contamination from other baboon samples.
source: The very low frequency of mismatches in the mapped reads from the mummified sample and its unique sequence are further evidence against the concern of contamination from other baboon samples.
evidence: Analysis of sequence data to assess contamination.

claim: The phylogenetic analysis produced tree topologies in agreement with those of prior studies, with three well-supported clades across the northeastern distribution of Papio (Roos et al., 2021).
source: Our phylogenetic analysis of the newly generated mitogenomes in combination with published mitochondrial sequence data produced tree topologies in agreement with those of prior studies, with three well-supported clades across the northeastern distribution of Papio (Roos et al., 2021).
evidence: Comparison of current phylogenetic results with prior research.

claim: The study reports mitochondrial sequence data of baboons from regions previously unstudied, namely South Sudan and Sudan.
source: For instance, we report mitochondrial sequence data of baboons from regions previously unstudied, namely South Sudan and Sudan.
evidence: Statement of novel geographic sampling.

claim: Samples from South and southern Sudan, east of the White Nile, nest within the central olive baboon clade J.
source: We show that samples from South and southern Sudan, east of the White Nile, nest within the central olive baboon clade J, whereas samples from the coastal region of Sudan and east of the Blue Nile nest within the hamadryas clade G3.
evidence: Phylogenetic result from the study.

claim: Samples from the coastal region of Sudan and east of the Blue Nile nest within the hamadryas clade G3.
source: We show that samples from South and southern Sudan, east of the White Nile, nest within the central olive baboon clade J, whereas samples from the coastal region of Sudan and east of the Blue Nile nest within the hamadryas clade G3.
evidence: Phylogenetic result from the study.

claim: These findings expand the northern distributions of both clade J and clade G3 significantly.
source: These findings expand the northern distributions of both clade J and clade G3 significantly, while also highlighting a strong geographic affinity between clade J and the Albertine Rift and (White) Nile Valley.
evidence: Interpretation of phylogenetic results in geographic context.

claim: The findings highlight a strong geographic affinity between clade J and the Albertine Rift and (White) Nile Valley.
source: These findings expand the northern distributions of both clade J and clade G3 significantly, while also highlighting a strong geographic affinity between clade J and the Albertine Rift and (White) Nile Valley.
evidence: Interpretation of phylogenetic results in geographic context.

claim: Clade J corresponds taxonomically with two subspecies recognized by Hill, 1970: P. a. heuglini and P. a. tesselatum.
source: Taxonomically, this clade corresponds with two subspecies recognized by Hill, 1970: P. a. heuglini and P. a. tesselatum.
evidence: Taxonomic interpretation based on phylogenetic results and cited taxonomy.

claim: The mummified hamadryas baboon from Gabbanat el-Qurud (MHNL 51000172) fell unequivocally in subclade G3-Y.
source: A mummified hamadryas baboon from Gabbanat el-Qurud (MHNL 51000172) yielded sufficient aDNA to produce a complete mitogenome, which fell unequivocally in subclade G3-Y (cf. Kopp et al., 2014b).
evidence: Phylogenetic result from the study.

claim: Subclade G3-Y consists of P. hamadryas and P. anubis samples from Eritrea and P. anubis samples from neighbouring regions in Sudan.
source: Haplotype networks allowed us to further refine subclade G3-Y, which consists of P. hamadryas and P. anubis samples from Eritrea and P. anubis samples from neighbouring regions in Sudan.
evidence: Result from haplotype network analysis.

claim: G3-Y also includes samples from the southern-most distribution of P. hamadryas on the Arabian Peninsula.
source: G3-Y also includes samples from the southern-most distribution of P. hamadryas on the Arabian Peninsula.
evidence: Result from haplotype network analysis.

claim: Geographic stability of phylogenetic clades over millennia has been shown for other baboon populations (Mathieson et al., 2020).
source: Geographic stability of phylogenetic clades over millennia has been shown for other baboon populations (Mathieson et al., 2020), leading us to infer that MHNL 51000172 (or its maternal ancestor) originated in the region where clade G3-Y exists today.
evidence: Citation of prior research supporting the inference.

claim: MHNL 51000172 (or its maternal ancestor) originated in the region where clade G3-Y exists today.
source: Geographic stability of phylogenetic clades over millennia has been shown for other baboon populations (Mathieson et al., 2020), leading us to infer that MHNL 51000172 (or its maternal ancestor) originated in the region where clade G3-Y exists today.
evidence: Inference based on phylogenetic results and assumption of geographic stability.

claim: An Arabian origin for MHNL 51000172 is unlikely based on the tight clustering of currently available Arabian sequences and distances in the HVRI network.
source: We cannot completely rule out an Arabian origin for MHNL 51000172, as our data does not cover the entire historic and present haplotype diversity there, but the tight clustering of the currently available Arabian sequences and distances in the HVRI network make an Arabian origin of MHNL 51000172 unlikely.
evidence: Inference based on haplotype network analysis.

claim: MHNL 51000172 was identified phenotypically as P. hamadryas (Lortet and Gaillard, 1907).
source: However, MHNL 51000172 was identified phenotypically as P. hamadryas (Lortet and Gaillard, 1907), and the distribution of hamadryas baboons is restricted to more eastern regions (Figure 2).
evidence: Historical taxonomic identification from Lortet and Gaillard, 1907.

claim: The distribution of hamadryas baboons is restricted to more eastern regions.
source: However, MHNL 51000172 was identified phenotypically as P. hamadryas (Lortet and Gaillard, 1907), and the distribution of hamadryas baboons is restricted to more eastern regions (Figure 2).
evidence: Geographic information shown in Figure 2.

claim: If the distributions of baboons in northeastern Africa have remained roughly stable within the last 2500 y, the region in Sudan east of the Blue Nile and west of the Atbarah River could not have served as a source region for hamadryas baboons.
source: If the distributions of baboons in northeastern Africa have remained roughly stable within the last 2500 y (as supported by ecological niche modelling; Chala et al., 2019), the region in Sudan east of the Blue Nile and west of the Atbarah River could not have served as a source region for hamadryas baboons.
evidence: Conditional inference based on assumption of geographic stability and ecological niche modeling.

claim: Ecological niche modelling supports that the distributions of baboons in northeastern Africa have remained roughly stable within the last 2500 y (Chala et al., 2019).
source: If the distributions of baboons in northeastern Africa have remained roughly stable within the last 2500 y (as supported by ecological niche modelling; Chala et al., 2019), the region in Sudan east of the Blue Nile and west of the Atbarah River could not have served as a source region for hamadryas baboons.
evidence: Citation of ecological niche modeling study.

claim: MHNL 51000172 (or its maternal ancestor) was captured in present-day Eritrea (or close neighbouring regions) and trafficked to Egypt.
source: Thus, it stands to reason that MHNL 51000172 (or its maternal ancestor) was captured in present-day Eritrea (or close neighbouring regions) and trafficked to Egypt.
evidence: Inference based on phylogenetic results and geographic distribution.

claim: The finding connects the mummified baboon to populations that live today in Eritrea and eastern Sudan, between 13° and 20° latitude.
source: The value of this finding is twofold. First, it connects the mummified baboon to populations that live today in Eritrea and eastern Sudan, between 13° and 20° latitude.
evidence: Summary of phylogenetic result in geographic terms.

claim: The finding corroborates the reports of Greco-Roman historians, who described Eritrea, and specifically Adulis, as the sole source of P. hamadryas for Ptolemaic Egyptians.
source: Second, it corroborates the reports of Greco-Roman historians, who described Eritrea, and specifically Adulis, as the sole source of P. hamadryas for Ptolemaic Egyptians.
evidence: Interpretation connecting genetic results with historical accounts.

claim: The mummified baboon predates the reign of Ptolemy I by centuries, presuming it is contemporaneous with another baboon (MHNL 90001206) dated to ca. 800–540 BCE (Richardin et al., 2017).
source: Yet, this baboon predates the reign of Ptolemy I by centuries, presuming it is contemporaneous with another baboon (MHNL 90001206) in the same assemblage, ca. 800–540 BCE (Richardin et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference based on radiometric dating of associated specimen.

claim: The findings raise the possibility that Adulis already existed as a trading centre or entrepôt during the 25th and 26th dynasties of Egypt.
source: Thus, our findings raise the possibility that Adulis already existed as a trading centre or entrepôt during the 25th and 26th dynasties of Egypt.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the dating and origin of the mummified baboon.

claim: Manzo, 2010 and others (Zazzaro et al., 2014) reassessed the ceramic tradition at Adulis and developed a chronology that stretches to the early second millennium BCE.
source: Manzo, 2010 and others (Zazzaro et al., 2014) reassessed the ceramic tradition at Adulis and developed a chronology that stretches to the early second millennium BCE, the deepest levels of which contained a fragment of blue glass with yellow inlays similar to Egyptian glass from the New Kingdom (Fattovich, 2018).
evidence: Citation of archaeological research on Adulis.

claim: The deepest levels of the ceramic tradition at Adulis contained a fragment of blue glass with yellow inlays similar to Egyptian glass from the New Kingdom (Fattovich, 2018).
source: Manzo, 2010 and others (Zazzaro et al., 2014) reassessed the ceramic tradition at Adulis and developed a chronology that stretches to the early second millennium BCE, the deepest levels of which contained a fragment of blue glass with yellow inlays similar to Egyptian glass from the New Kingdom (Fattovich, 2018).
evidence: Archaeological evidence cited from Fattovich, 2018.

claim: Contact between Egypt and the Eritrean lowlands is attested by trade goods dating to ca. 1800–1650 BCE or earlier, including potsherds, obsidian, and fragments of carbonized ebony (Fattovich, 2018; Lucarini et al., 2020).
source: In Egypt, contact with the Eritrean lowlands is attested by trade goods dating to ca. 1800–1650 BCE or earlier, including potsherds, obsidian, and fragments of carbonized ebony (Fattovich, 2018; Lucarini et al., 2020).
evidence: Archaeological evidence cited from multiple sources.

claim: Trade goods from the Eritrean lowlands were discovered at Mersa Gawasis, a Middle Kingdom harbour.
source: Discovered at Mersa Gawasis, a Middle Kingdom harbour, these artefacts appear to align the prehistory of Adulis with the fabled Land of Punt (Bard and Fattovich, 2018; Manzo, 2010; Manzo, 2012), an enigmatic toponym scattered across scant and disconnected records (Cooper, 2020).
evidence: Archaeological context cited from multiple sources.

claim: Artefacts from Mersa Gawasis appear to align the prehistory of Adulis with the fabled Land of Punt (Bard and Fattovich, 2018; Manzo, 2010; Manzo, 2012).
source: Discovered at Mersa Gawasis, a Middle Kingdom harbour, these artefacts appear to align the prehistory of Adulis with the fabled Land of Punt (Bard and Fattovich, 2018; Manzo, 2010; Manzo, 2012), an enigmatic toponym scattered across scant and disconnected records (Cooper, 2020).
evidence: Interpretation of archaeological evidence with citations.

claim: Punt existed in a region south and east of Egypt, and was accessible by land or sea.
source: Punt existed in a region south and east of Egypt, and was accessible by land or sea.
evidence: Historical knowledge about Punt.

claim: For Egyptians, Punt was a source of 'marvels,' particularly incense, but also baboons, that drove bidirectional trade for 1300 y (ca. 2500–1170 BCE) (Tallet, 2013).
source: For Egyptians, Punt was a source of 'marvels,' particularly incense, but also baboons, that drove bidirectional trade for 1300 y (ca. 2500–1170 BCE) (Tallet, 2013).
evidence: Historical information cited from Tallet, 2013.

claim: Some scholars have described the trade with Punt as the beginning of economic globalization (Fattovich, 2012).
source: Some scholars have described this enterprise as the beginning of economic globalization (Fattovich, 2012), whereas others view it as the earliest maritime leg of the spice route (Keay, 2006), a trade network that would shape geopolitical fortunes for millennia.
evidence: Scholarly interpretation cited from Fattovich, 2012.

claim: Some scholars view the trade with Punt as the earliest maritime leg of the spice route (Keay, 2006).
source: Some scholars have described this enterprise as the beginning of economic globalization (Fattovich, 2012), whereas others view it as the earliest maritime leg of the spice route (Keay, 2006), a trade network that would shape geopolitical fortunes for millennia.
evidence: Scholarly interpretation cited from Keay, 2006.

claim: The location of Punt is uncertain, in part because the toponym fades from view after the early first millennium BCE.
source: The global historical importance of Punt is therefore considerable, but there is a problem—its location is uncertain, in part because the toponym fades from view. From the early first millennium BCE, there are no further records of Egyptians in Punt or of Puntites visiting Egypt.
evidence: Historical observation about the disappearance of Punt from records.

claim: From the early first millennium BCE, there are no further records of Egyptians in Punt or of Puntites visiting Egypt.
source: The global historical importance of Punt is therefore considerable, but there is a problem—its location is uncertain, in part because the toponym fades from view. From the early first millennium BCE, there are no further records of Egyptians in Punt or of Puntites visiting Egypt.
evidence: Historical observation about the absence of records.

claim: There are two incomplete inscriptions that mention Punt in a narrative context, both attributed to the 26th (Saite) Dynasty (Betrò, 1996; Cavasin, 2019).
source: There are, however, two incomplete inscriptions that mention Punt in a narrative context, and both are attributed to the 26th (Saite) Dynasty (Betrò, 1996; Cavasin, 2019).
evidence: Historical information cited from Betrò, 1996 and Cavasin, 2019.

claim: The Defenneh stele describes an expedition to Punt that was saved from dying thirst by unexpected rainfall on 'the mountains of Punt' (Meeks, 2003).
source: One of these, the Defenneh stele, describes an expedition to Punt that was saved from dying thirst by unexpected rainfall on 'the mountains of Punt' (Meeks, 2003).
evidence: Historical account cited from Meeks, 2003.

claim: The Defenneh stele is a testament to the efforts of Saitic pharaohs to revive maritime commerce on the Red Sea (Lloyd, 1977).
source: The Defenneh stele is a testament to the efforts of Saitic pharaohs to revive maritime commerce on the Red Sea (Lloyd, 1977), while also raising the possibility of renewed trade with Punt.
evidence: Historical interpretation cited from Lloyd, 1977.

claim: The Saite dynasty existed from 664–525 BCE.
source: It is perhaps no coincidence that the Saite dynasty (664–525 BCE) exists squarely within the radiometric date range of hamadryas baboons from Gabbanat el-Qurud.
evidence: Historical dating information.

claim: The Saite dynasty (664–525 BCE) exists squarely within the radiometric date range of hamadryas baboons from Gabbanat el-Qurud.
source: It is perhaps no coincidence that the Saite dynasty (664–525 BCE) exists squarely within the radiometric date range of hamadryas baboons from Gabbanat el-Qurud.
evidence: Temporal correlation between historical period and specimen dating.

claim: Punt, like Adulis, was a source of baboons for Egyptians.
source: Punt, like Adulis, was a source of baboons for Egyptians, a history that raises the possibility of using baboons as a tool for testing geographic hypotheses.
evidence: Historical knowledge about Punt and Adulis.

claim: Dominy et al., 2020 used stable isotope mapping methods to determine the geoprovenance of mummified baboons from Thebes dated to the (late) New Kingdom.
source: Recently, Dominy et al., 2020 used stable isotope mapping methods to determine the geoprovenance of mummified baboons from Thebes (modern-day Luxor) and dated to the (late) New Kingdom.
evidence: Citation of prior research methods and findings.

claim: Dominy et al., 2020 results pointed to present-day Ethiopia, Eritrea, or Djibouti, as well as portions of Somalia as the origin of New Kingdom baboons.
source: Their results pointed to present-day Ethiopia, Eritrea, or Djibouti, as well as portions of Somalia, an area that corroborates most scholarly views on the location of Punt (Breyer, 2016; Kitchen, 2004), but see Meeks, 2002; Meeks, 2003; Tallet, 2013.
evidence: Citation of prior research findings.

claim: The results of Dominy et al., 2020 corroborate most scholarly views on the location of Punt (Breyer, 2016; Kitchen, 2004).
source: Their results pointed to present-day Ethiopia, Eritrea, or Djibouti, as well as portions of Somalia, an area that corroborates most scholarly views on the location of Punt (Breyer, 2016; Kitchen, 2004), but see Meeks, 2002; Meeks, 2003; Tallet, 2013.
evidence: Comparison of research findings with scholarly consensus.

claim: The study used aDNA to show that at least one baboon from the 25th Dynasty or Late Period can be traced to Eritrea.
source: Here, we used aDNA to show that at least one baboon from the 25th Dynasty or Late Period of Egyptian history—a span that coincides with the last known expeditions to Punt, but predates Greco-Roman accounts of Adulis as a source of baboons—can be traced to Eritrea.
evidence: Summary of the study's main finding.

claim: The 25th Dynasty or Late Period coincides with the last known expeditions to Punt, but predates Greco-Roman accounts of Adulis as a source of baboons.
source: Here, we used aDNA to show that at least one baboon from the 25th Dynasty or Late Period of Egyptian history—a span that coincides with the last known expeditions to Punt, but predates Greco-Roman accounts of Adulis as a source of baboons—can be traced to Eritrea.
evidence: Historical context connecting different time periods.

claim: The findings appear to establish primatological continuity between Punt and Adulis.
source: Thus, our findings appear to establish primatological continuity between Punt and Adulis.
evidence: Interpretation of the study's findings in historical context.

claim: The findings bolster recurrent conjecture among some historical archaeologists that Punt and Adulis were essentially the same trading centre from different eras of Egyptian antiquity (Doresse, 1959; Fattovich, 2018; Kitchen, 2004; Massa, 2021; Phillips, 1997; Sleeswyk, 1983).
source: Such a conclusion must be viewed with caution, but it bolsters recurrent conjecture among some historical archaeologists: that Punt and Adulis were essentially the same trading centre from different eras of Egyptian antiquity (Doresse, 1959; Fattovich, 2018; Kitchen, 2004; Massa, 2021; Phillips, 1997; Sleeswyk, 1983).
evidence: Interpretation connecting findings with scholarly speculation, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The results reinforce the view that ancient Egyptian mariners travelled great distances to acquire living baboons.
source: At minimum, our results reinforce the view that ancient Egyptian mariners travelled great distances to acquire living baboons.
evidence: Interpretation of findings in historical context.

claim: The study discarded seven historic samples and nine mummified samples due to insufficient DNA content, sequencing failure, or low coverage and sequencing depth.
source: We discarded seven historic samples and nine mummified samples from our analysis due to insufficient DNA content, sequencing failure, or low coverage and sequencing depth (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Description of sample exclusion criteria and results.

claim: The study obtained 896,025,770 raw sequence reads in total.
source: In total, we obtained 896,025,770 raw sequence reads, with a mean of 34,462,530 (± SD 27,945,321) raw sequence reads per sample.
evidence: Sequencing data summary.

claim: On average, 95.5% of reads survived trimming.
source: On average, 95.5% of reads survived trimming and a median of 9934 (range: 244–2,722,354) reads per sample mapped to the reference mitogenome.
evidence: Data processing result.

claim: A median of 9934 (range: 244–2,722,354) reads per sample mapped to the reference mitogenome.
source: On average, 95.5% of reads survived trimming and a median of 9934 (range: 244–2,722,354) reads per sample mapped to the reference mitogenome.
evidence: Mapping result summary.

claim: After removal of duplicates, a median of 7398 (range: 237–497,458) mapped reads per sample resulted in the median final sequencing depth of 26× (range: 0.21–2952×).
source: After removal of duplicates (duplication level median: 25.1%; range: 2.5–92.6%), a median of 7398 (range: 237–497,458) mapped reads per sample resulted in the median final sequencing depth of 26× (range: 0.21–2952×).
evidence: Data processing and sequencing depth results.

claim: After exclusion of samples with low quality, the final dataset had a median final sequencing depth of 37× (range: 16–2952×).
source: After exclusion of samples with low quality, the final dataset had a median final sequencing depth of 37× (range: 16–2952×), with a median of 0.4% undetermined sites (range: 0–1.7%) and a median breadth of coverage of at least 3× of 99.3% (range: 97.4–100%) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Final dataset quality metrics.

claim: Capture enrichment strongly increased the number of mapped reads and final mean coverage compared to the shotgun approach.
source: Capture enrichment strongly increased the number of mapped reads and final mean coverage compared to the shotgun approach (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: Comparison of sequencing methods shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: GC content of sequences was 40–50% in the same range as the reference genomes.
source: GC content of sequences was 40–50% (Figure 5) in the same range as the reference genomes.
evidence: GC content analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The sequencing reads of the mummified sample (MHNL51000172) exhibit C to T and G to A misincorporations at 5′ and 3′ ends, reaching frequencies of 3.3 and 1.6% at the first/last position of the read.
source: The sequencing reads of the mummified sample (MHNL51000172) exhibit C to T and G to A misincorporations at 5′ and 3′ ends, reaching frequencies of 3.3 and 1.6% at the first/last position of the read (Figure 6).
evidence: DNA damage analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Phylogenetic trees inferred from maximum likelihood (ML) and Bayesian inference (BI) revealed identical topologies with generally strong node support (100% bootstrap support [BS] and posterior probability [PP] 1.0) and clearly defined geographic clades.
source: Phylogenetic trees inferred from maximum likelihood (ML) and Bayesian inference (BI) revealed identical topologies with generally strong node support (100% bootstrap support [BS] and posterior probability [PP] 1.0) and clearly defined geographic clades (Figure 8, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis results shown in Figure 8.

claim: Mitochondrial clades did not directly mirror species assignments.
source: These mitochondrial clades did not directly mirror species assignments.
evidence: Observation from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Within the northeastern baboons, the central olive baboon clade J from Democratic Republic of the Congo, Tanzania, South Sudan, and southern Sudan diverged first.
source: Within the northeastern baboons, the central olive baboon clade J from Democratic Republic of the Congo, Tanzania, South Sudan, and southern Sudan diverged first, followed by northern yellow baboons of clade G1 including a sample from Somalia.
evidence: Phylogenetic result from the study.

claim: Northern yellow baboons of clade G1 including a sample from Somalia diverged after clade J.
source: Within the northeastern baboons, the central olive baboon clade J from Democratic Republic of the Congo, Tanzania, South Sudan, and southern Sudan diverged first, followed by northern yellow baboons of clade G1 including a sample from Somalia.
evidence: Phylogenetic result from the study.

claim: Hamadryas baboons formed clade G3, which also included olive baboons from the region.
source: Hamadryas baboons formed clade G3, which also included olive baboons from the region.
evidence: Phylogenetic result from the study.

source: Clade G3 contained three subclades: subclade G3-Z comprised hamadryas baboons from Ethiopia and Djibouti; subclade G3-X comprised hamadryas and olive baboons from Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Somalia; and subclade G3-Y comprised hamadryas and olive baboons from northeastern Sudan and Eritrea.
evidence: Phylogenetic result from the study.

claim: Subclade G3-X comprised hamadryas and olive baboons from Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Somalia.
source: Clade G3 contained three subclades: subclade G3-Z comprised hamadryas baboons from Ethiopia and Djibouti; subclade G3-X comprised hamadryas and olive baboons from Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Somalia; and subclade G3-Y comprised hamadryas and olive baboons from northeastern Sudan and Eritrea.
evidence: Phylogenetic result from the study.

claim: Subclade G3-Y comprised hamadryas and olive baboons from northeastern Sudan and Eritrea.
source: Clade G3 contained three subclades: subclade G3-Z comprised hamadryas baboons from Ethiopia and Djibouti; subclade G3-X comprised hamadryas and olive baboons from Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Somalia; and subclade G3-Y comprised hamadryas and olive baboons from northeastern Sudan and Eritrea.
evidence: Phylogenetic result from the study.

claim: The mummified baboon from Gabbanat el-Qurud was located in subclade G3-Y, closely related to samples from Eritrea and northeastern Sudan.
source: The mummified baboon from Gabbanat el-Qurud (MHNL 51000172) was located in subclade G3-Y, closely related to samples from Eritrea and northeastern Sudan.
evidence: Phylogenetic result from the study.

claim: Individuals closely related to the mummified baboon in the cyt b network were those from Sudan (on the Red Sea coast and in Senaar), Eritrea (between 14.3–16.0N 36.7–39.0E), and the Arabian Peninsula.
source: Individuals closely related to this mummified baboon in the cyt b network were those from Sudan (on the Red Sea coast and in Senaar), Eritrea (between 14.3–16.0N 36.7–39.0E), and the Arabian Peninsula (Figure 9—figure supplement 1), and in the HVRI network samples from location 'Bbr' (Barka Bridge, 15.6N 38.0E) in Eritrea (Figure 9).
evidence: Haplotype network analysis result shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the HVRI network, samples closely related to the mummified baboon were from location 'Bbr' (Barka Bridge, 15.6N 38.0E) in Eritrea.
source: Individuals closely related to this mummified baboon in the cyt b network were those from Sudan (on the Red Sea coast and in Senaar), Eritrea (between 14.3–16.0N 36.7–39.0E), and the Arabian Peninsula (Figure 9—figure supplement 1), and in the HVRI network samples from location 'Bbr' (Barka Bridge, 15.6N 38.0E) in Eritrea (Figure 9).

claim: Direct radiocarbon dating of MHNL 51000172 and other baboons from Gabbanat el-Qurud is an urgent priority.
source: Direct radiocarbon dating of MHNL 51000172 and other baboons from Gabbanat el-Qurud is an urgent priority, in part because doing so would put these specimens into conversation with those from the catacombs of Tuna el-Gebel.
evidence: Recommendation for future research.

claim: The oldest gallery at Tuna el-Gebel, Gallery D, is dated to the 26th Dynasty and contains a single species of baboon: P. anubis.
source: The oldest gallery at Tuna el-Gebel, Gallery D, is dated to the 26th Dynasty and contains a single species of baboon: P. anubis.
evidence: Archaeological information about Tuna el-Gebel.

claim: Some scholars (Peters, 2020; von den Driesch et al., 2004) have argued that olive baboons from Gallery D at Tuna el-Gebel, as well as Chlorocebus aethiops, were sourced from the Sudanese Nile Valley and adjacent areas.
source: Some scholars (Peters, 2020; von den Driesch et al., 2004) have argued that these olive baboons, as well as Chlorocebus aethiops (also found in Gallery D), were sourced from the Sudanese Nile Valley and adjacent areas, which predicts membership in clade G3-Y, although clade J is also plausible.
evidence: Citation of scholarly arguments about baboon origins.

claim: Construction of Gallery C at Tuna el-Gebel began during the first period of Persian rule in Egypt (524–404 BCE) and continued through the 30th and Ptolemaic dynasties.
source: Construction of Gallery C began during the first period of Persian rule in Egypt (524–404 BCE) and continued through the 30th and Ptolemaic dynasties.
evidence: Archaeological and historical information about Tuna el-Gebel.

claim: Every phase of Gallery C at Tuna el-Gebel contains mummified specimens of both P. anubis and P. hamadryas.
source: As every phase of Gallery C contains mummified specimens of both P. anubis and P. hamadryas, there is rich opportunity to explore diachronic changes in trade routes using phylogeographic methods.
evidence: Archaeological observation about Gallery C.
